stem: A nurse is caring for a monitored client whose usual heart rate is above the unit's default high-alarm threshold. Which approach best supports alarm safety?

options.A: Leave every default limit unchanged even when it produces repeated nonactionable alarms.
options.B: Silence the alarm permanently so it cannot recur.
options.C: Tailor alarm limits to the individual client's clinical condition within approved policy while preserving clinically meaningful alerts.
options.D: Disable all physiologic alarms whenever the client has a chronic abnormal baseline.

rationale: AHRQ patient-safety guidance identifies alarm settings that are not tailored to individual patients as a contributor to alarm fatigue and recommends tailoring alarm thresholds when default settings do not fit the patient's clinical baseline. Alarms should remain clinically meaningful rather than being permanently silenced. Therefore C is correct.
educational_objective: Apply individualized, policy-consistent physiologic alarm settings to reduce nonactionable alarms without compromising patient safety.
source_organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) PSNet
source_locator: What can be done to combat alarm fatigue?; Take-Home Points — tailor alarm thresholds to the individual patient
source_claim_supported: Default alarm settings may not fit an individual patient; clinicians can tailor alarm thresholds to the individual clinical baseline to reduce excessive nonactionable alarms, while alarms should not simply be silenced.
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — monitoring equipment, alarm safety and error prevention
correction_summary: The original Joint Commission citation did not directly surface the patient-level alarm-setting claim in current public NPG text. Re-sourced the semantic claim to AHRQ PSNet, retained current NCSBN blueprint authority, and rewrote the item to explicitly require policy-consistent individualized limits rather than unrestricted bedside adjustment. Difficulty set to medium.
audit_findings: AHRQ directly supports patient-specific alarm thresholds and warns against silencing. C preserves policy boundaries and meaningful alarms; A, B and D create alarm-fatigue or missed-event risk. Independent second pass passed.
